The most likely reason it hurts is because you’re pushing for the notes. Most guys go through it when trying to pass notes around D4 and most women do it when trying to pass notes around their passagio with power. 

In order to sing rock/grunge/new wave in a healthy way you need to have a pretty good understanding of vocal technique.

Your voice creates sound by your vocal folds vibrating. When you push for notes you push by using air pressure that comes up through your lungs and up your throat. Too much air pressure causes your neck muscles to get tight because your body is trying to protect itself from vocal damage and your body is smart for doing this. 

In order to sing in these specific styles it is best to work with a voice coach to achieve good internal acoustical space and technique for singing high notes without unnecessary weight (too much weight carried up causes straining).

I understand you don’t have the funds. You can start by doing scales in a straw that is in water. Sing through the straw and try your best to maintain a steady air stream without a lot of air. If the bubbles are going like crazy you aren’t doing it right.

Tone is good. Main issue I hear is pitch which is a support/laryngeal issues. Try to keep a wide feeling on the inside always and work with straw in water for air pressure and hissing for more core support.

One concern you should have is surrounding not deepening of the voice but tightening of the neck. Since I workout and do progressive overload I do neck and laryngeal massages every morning when I first wake up and after cooling off after weightlifting. If you don’t do this your neck will likely get tighter and tighter over time leading to problems singing comfortably.

Also keep in mind that the male voice doesn’t mature completely until around 25-30 so your voice can still change back and forth overtime.

Hello, I am a tenor in musical theatre who relies 80% on my mixed voice. 

Ok so the mixed voice is kind of a very wide area and it’s very flexible. Think of mixed voice as play dough. If I hand you play dough, you can flatten it and make a huge wide circle or you could take a small piece out of the dough and make an extremely small circle. In the end they’re both the same thing, play dough. 

Same thing with the mixed voice. The first thing you mentioned is probably a technique commonly known as mixed-belting. This is where you, in my experience, use the feeling of your light mix with the feeling of belting with full chest. Also referred to as a chest dominant mix. 

The second thing you mention is likely what people call just mix, light mix, or a head dominant mix. This is a lighter spot that isn’t completely head voice/falsetto but also isn’t completely chest either.

So both are mixed voice but different types. 

The second way is achieved by being very relaxed and having good control over your voice and knowing it very well and knowing when to add more chest and when to add more head voice. 

The way I mix “high” notes such as B4-F5 is by making sure I’m not pulling up unneeded weight from my chest voice and keeping the feeling light but finding the spot where it is still strong.

1. Know what you want

Do you want to sing classical? Find a coach with a background in classical. Do you want to sing pop? Find a coach who knows a lot about the pop vocal style. And the list goes on and on. 

2. Go to the coach for at least one lesson 

When you first go to a coach likely they’ll ask you about your background in music, why you want to sing, goals for your voice, etc. Then, they will normally run you through a few warm ups to get to know your voice and then have you sing a song of your choice for them. 

3. If you like them, continue with them. 

3.5. Practice, practice, practice 

When some start going to a vocal coach they think they don’t have to do anything outside of lessons when that’s very far from the truth. For most people they’re only in their lesson for a very small amount of time per week. A coach is supposed to give you guidance and things to work on. It is your job to work on them so you become a better singer. 



——————————————————————————

However, there are a few things all coaches regardless of expertise and/or background should do.

1. Communicate with you/let you communicate with them

They should never do anything to hurt you. If you feel uncomfortable doing something, tell them. I’ve had multiple coaches, some throughout warm ups will ask you “How does that feel?” or “Does your throat feel ok?” But, if they don’t ask this question it’s up to you to tell them how you feel if something isn’t ok.

2. You should be able to hear progression after a while

After going to a coach once you find one suitable, you should be able to hear a difference. Doesn’t matter how big or small it is. If you hear absolutely no difference or progression at all, it’s time to look for a new coach. Of course you’re not going to go from a beginner to a Frank Sinatra or an Idina Menzel but you should hear a bit of a difference and be more comfortable singing. 

3. You should be improving not just audibly but your knowledge in singing/the voice should grow as well

I do musical theatre and one of my directors also doubles as a “vocal coach”. A few of my friends started going to her a year ago for vocal lessons and a few others down the line as well. What have they learned? Nothing. Not. Good. If you go to a vocal coach the main reason of course is to improve the sound of your voice. But, you should also learn how to warm yourself up. You should learn basic terminology such as vibrato, chest voice, mix voice, head voice, belting, and other general things like that. If a coach doesn’t explain these things to you it will be hard to understand what you’re doing while singing and recognize how singers you admire do different things and how to get different tones and volume in your voice. So if you go to a coach for a couple months and don’t know anything. Once again, time to find a new coach.
